content: An aphthous ulcer, also known as a canker sore, is a painful open sore that occurs inside the mouth due to a disruption in the mucous membrane. This condition is also referred to as aphthous stomatitis and, in cases of multiple or recurring ulcers, may be called Sutton's Disease. The term aphthae was first introduced by Hippocrates between 460 and 370 B.C. to describe disorders of the mouth. Aphthous ulcers are categorized into three types: major aphthous stomatitis, minor aphthous stomatitis, and herpetiform stomatitis. The exact mechanism behind the development of aphthous ulcers is not fully understood. Theories include cross-reactivity between microbial antigens and mitochondrial heat shock proteins, dysembryoplastic processes, histopathological changes in glandular cells, or thrombotic events. Factors that predispose individuals to these ulcers include trauma, cessation of smoking, stress, hormonal imbalances, and food hypersensitivities. The precise cause of aphthous ulcers remains unknown. However, several triggers have been identified, such as stress, fatigue, illness, accidental biting, hormonal fluctuations, menstruation, rapid weight loss, food allergies, sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) in toothpaste, and deficiencies in vitamin B12, iron, or folic acid. It is important to distinguish aphthous ulcers from other conditions, such as malignant ulcers, infections, rheumatic diseases, and cutaneous disorders. The prevalence of aphthous ulcers is estimated to range from 1,000 to 60,000 cases per 100,000 individuals annually, affecting both adults and children. Risk factors for recurrent aphthous ulcers include the use of dentures or braces, gender, age, family history, oral diseases, and stress. Routine screening for aphthous ulcers is not recommended. However, patients with XY gonadal abnormalities should undergo sonographic monitoring starting at age 2, every six months, until the gonads are surgically removed. The progression, complications, and prognosis of recurrent aphthous ulcers vary depending on the severity of the condition. There is no single diagnostic test for aphthous ulcers. Symptoms typically include oral pain, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), and the presence of oral lesions that may have resolved spontaneously in the past. On physical examination, aphthous ulcers may appear as shallow or deep lesions, occurring in small numbers (1-5) or large numbers (5-100). They may or may not leave scars, and these features help in classifying the condition. There are no specific laboratory, electrocardiographic, X-ray, ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or other imaging findings associated with aphthous ulcers. Similarly, no other diagnostic studies are available for this condition. Most cases of aphthous ulcers resolve on their own within 1 to 2 weeks and require only supportive care. Maintaining good oral hygiene is essential. Spicy, acidic, and salty foods and beverages should be avoided, as they can exacerbate pain and irritation. Strong mouthwashes, such as Listerine, may also cause irritation and are generally discouraged during an active ulcer episode. Surgical treatment is not recommended for managing aphthous ulcers. There is no established method for preventing aphthous ulcers. However, maintaining good dental hygiene and attending regular dental check-ups are strongly advised to promote oral health and reduce the risk of developing these ulcers.
